findings.title: Login timing side channel enables username enumeration
findings.rootCause: Lookup short-circuits before scrypt when the username does not exist, so response time differs between existing and missing users even though both return the same 401 code.
findings.confidenceRationale: Direct source reading; scrypt runs only for existing users, a measurable difference. No runtime measurement performed in this offline static run.
findings.impact: Attacker can distinguish valid usernames and build an account list for credential stuffing.
findings.scenario: POST login for candidate usernames and compare latency; valid names take scrypt time, invalid names return immediately.
findings.recommendation: Always perform a scrypt verification against a dummy hash when the user is missing, and compare with timing-safe equality.

challenge.callers: checked the only caller (router login handler)
challenge.controls: same 401 code and message for both branches
challenge.counterevidence: rate limiting absent, so attacker can sample repeatedly
challenge.conclusion: survives challenge; message equality does not hide timing

findings.title: No login rate limiting or account lockout
findings.rootCause: The login route performs credential checks on every request with no per-IP or per-account throttle.
findings.confidenceRationale: No rate-limit middleware exists; SPEC/PRD explicitly excludes it.
findings.impact: Online password guessing is unbounded; weak demo passwords are trivially brute-forced.
findings.scenario: Concurrent login attempts against userA with a password wordlist.
findings.recommendation: Add bounded per-account/IP rate limiting and backoff before shipping outside a local demo.

challenge.controls: no throttle or lockout in code or config
challenge.counterevidence: PRD states this is out of scope; still a real weakness for any non-local use
challenge.conclusion: survives challenge as a scoped limitation

findings.title: Sessions never expire and are not revocable except logout
findings.rootCause: sessions table has no expires_at and auth check does not validate age; cookies have no Max-Age but server-side rows persist indefinitely.
findings.confidenceRationale: Schema and createSession show no expiry field or cleanup.
findings.attackerControl: Stolen session cookie (e.g., from a shared machine or log)
findings.impact: A stolen token remains valid until explicit logout, indefinitely.
findings.scenario: Copy fruitlab_session cookie from a logged-in browser and reuse it days later.
findings.recommendation: Add expires_at, enforce it on lookup, clean up expired rows, and document rotation.

challenge.controls: logout deletes the row, but no age check exists
challenge.counterevidence: PRD excludes expiry; local-only demo lowers exposure
challenge.conclusion: survives challenge as a scoped limitation

findings.title: Order ownership rejection discloses order-number existence
findings.rootCause: GET /api/orders/{orderNumber} returns 403 order-not-owned for existing orders of other users and 404 only for non-existent numbers.
findings.confidenceRationale: Response codes differ by existence; documented tradeoff D-32.
findings.attackerControl: Guessed order numbers with a valid session
findings.impact: Attacker can confirm whether an order number exists (limited enumeration).
findings.scenario: Iterate candidate FL-... numbers; 403 means exists, 404 means not.
findings.recommendation: Return 404 for other users' orders if existence disclosure matters; keep 403 only if teaching requires it and document the tradeoff.

challenge.counterevidence: D-32 records this as an intentional classroom tradeoff
challenge.conclusion: survives challenge; accepted risk, not a functional bug
